summary: This document recommends using TLS to protect email between a user's client and the mail submission or access server. It treats TLS from the start of connection as preferred over cleartext plus upgrade, and updates several earlier RFCs for POP3, IMAP and submission.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC recommends protecting email traffic between a mail client and its access or submission server with TLS. It prefers a TLS connection from the first step and calls for cleartext services to be phased out.

questions: should email clients use implicit tls
is starttls still recommended for email
subtitle: Recommends TLS for email submission and access, with a preference for TLS from connection start.

tldr.problem: Email clients and servers may use cleartext connections or fail to use TLS in ways that protect passwords and messages.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends TLS for all client-to-server submission and access traffic, deprecating cleartext and preferring Implicit TLS over STARTTLS where available.
tldr.outcome: It adds Implicit TLS service registrations and updates earlier POP, IMAP, submission and discovery guidance. RFC 8997 later updates it.

today: RFC 8314 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8997. It updates RFCs 1939, 2595, 3501, 5068, 6186 and 6409.

sections.title: Protecting Mail Access and Submission
sections.content:
The RFC covers TLS between a Mail User Agent (MUA) and a Mail Access Server or Mail Submission Server. It recommends TLS 1.2 or later for all such traffic and says providers should deprecate cleartext access and submission as soon as practicable.

It prefers Implicit TLS, where the TLS handshake begins when the TCP connection opens, over starting in cleartext and requesting a STARTTLS upgrade. It does not cover TLS for message relay between mail servers or replace end-to-end email encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Use TLS when a mail app accesses a mailbox or submits outgoing mail. The RFC prefers starting TLS immediately rather than beginning with a cleartext connection.

sections.title: Implicit TLS Services and Ports
sections.content:
Implicit TLS starts a TLS handshake as soon as a TCP connection opens on a port reserved for TLS. The RFC defines POP service pop3s on port 995, IMAP service imaps on port 993, and submission service submissions on port 465.

For a transition period, clients and servers should also support STARTTLS on submission port 587. The RFC says the two methods have no significant security difference when both implementations require successful TLS negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: With Implicit TLS, the connection begins with the security handshake. Each mail protocol has a designated service name and port for that connection.

sections.title: Server and Provider Requirements
sections.content:
Providers that offer POP, IMAP or message submission must provide TLS access, and servers must support TLS 1.2 or later. Providers should offer Implicit TLS and should keep STARTTLS available in the near term for older clients.

Cleartext access should be phased out and eventually disabled or restricted to legacy systems. After cleartext authentication is disabled, servers must not reveal on a cleartext channel whether credentials were valid. Providers must maintain valid server certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers must support current TLS and use valid certificates. Providers should reduce cleartext access over time and avoid revealing credential validity through an unprotected connection.

sections.title: Finding Servers with DNS
sections.content:
Providers should publish DNS SRV records that help mail clients find access and submission servers. Records for Implicit TLS services should be preferred over STARTTLS or cleartext services. RFC 8314 adds the _submissions._tcp service label.

Clients should check that SRV records are DNSSEC-signed or that the target name matches the queried domain. Clients must not consult unsigned SRV records on every connection attempt.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS can tell a mail app where secure mail services are available. Clients should check that the discovery information is trustworthy before relying on it.

sections.title: Mail Client Confidentiality Rules
sections.content:
Mail clients must implement TLS 1.2 or later and must validate server certificates. By default, a new account must require a valid certificate and should require TLS 1.1 or greater. A client must not send credentials unless the configured minimum confidentiality level is met.

A client may allow certificate pinning during account setup, but a pinned certificate does not meet the minimum confidentiality level because an attacker could interfere during setup. Clients must not reuse a pinned certificate for another account.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail app should not send a password until it has established the required protection and verified the server certificate. Trusting a certificate by pinning it during setup does not meet that protection level.

sections.title: Security Scope and Limits
sections.content:
The recommendations aim to reduce network snooping and interception, not attacks by someone who has compromised a provider's systems. Software that scans mail by intercepting the application connection can interfere unless its mail components follow these requirements.

Client certificates can reveal a user's identity to observers with TLS 1.2 and earlier, so clients should send them only when authorized. TLS protects the connection to the provider; it is not end-to-end encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS helps protect mail traffic from people observing the network. It does not protect against an attacker who has already compromised the mail provider.
